title: Miaoya Is Not an AI Native Product: It's Just an Internet Product That Uses AI Well
dek: Zhang Yueguang reviews two years of entrepreneurship: Miaoya traded user freedom for stable results, which is internet product thinking at heart; AI Native products need to shift to context-oriented design, and one-way-door products are what he's willing to bet everything on.
why: The first half is resume and Miaoya review, with average information density; the second half on AI Native, one-way doors, and the two value orientations of Agents is the truly valuable part of this episode.
who: Product managers and founders building AI applications and Agents, and investors who want to understand what "AI Native" actually means.
skip: The resume and first-startup review from 2:00-16:00 can be fast-forwarded; low information density.

points.h: Miaoya is not an AI Native product
points.body: Zhang Yueguang's broadest conclusion is: Miaoya is not an AI native product, it is an internet product that brings AI capabilities into full play. He refutes the popular definition that "a product that couldn't be made without this generation of AI technology is AI Native"—that is only a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The feature he adds is the openness of user input and output: the basic principle of twenty years of internet product design is process-oriented; users come in and there are five doors and five buttons, and the product manager, like a game designer, designs the flow, so user freedom is limited. Miaoya seeks more stable and better results precisely by limiting user freedom—fixed 20 photos, fixed templates, fixed generation process—which is essentially still internet product thinking.

points.h: From process design to context design
points.body: It took him two years to break through this thinking. The industrial collaboration paradigm of twenty years of the internet is linear: the product manager first defines what users can do, what they input, what they output; the designer turns the definition into a diagram; the engineer builds according to the diagram, like building a house. But in AI Native products no product manager can exhaust all possible user behaviors; you don't know what strange commands users will give, and for Agent-type products even the output is uncertain. So the collaboration method must be reversed: first figure out how user input brings in invisible context, what impact these contexts have in the generation step, and what the best context and best prompt practices are—this part becomes the most critical. Only after fully understanding this do you discuss what process to build for users.

points.h: Organization goes from linear to two-stage
points.body: He judges that AI organizations will see two changes. First, decision boundaries become blurred: it's hard to define that a product manager only does product and doesn't touch models and technology; tasks require a mix of multiple disciplines, designers need to understand what beauty is, product managers need their own taste, taste becomes very important, and this definition often cannot be given by a single discipline. Second, work goes from linear to two-stage: the first stage is exploring the model, and this process is bound to be chaotic and less regular; after everyone is very clear about what the model is used for and what context users need to provide, then enter the second stage of formal division of labor—product managers design the process to obtain context, designers cooperate, and then formal development begins. He also refutes the claim that "big companies find it hard to turn around and react slowly," considering it an illusion.

When he started the company he had only a vague vision: at the time all AI products existed as some kind of service or tool, but he felt this generation of AI technology should be a process of creating population—AI is an individual, an object, not a service. The slogan he adopted was "create AI friends," and he believes that at some point the AI population in this world should be larger than the human population, with or without bodies. These populations should, like humans, have the ability to obtain information, think, process information, publish information, and connect with others. He specifically went to talk with friends at Hupan: can you start a company without a clear mission? The other party said that a company like Mr. Ma's that proposed "make it easy to do business anywhere" on day one is very rare; the vast majority of successful companies had no mission or vision at the start, and many missions are gradually carved out during the process.

points.h: Three common industry problems of AI companionship
points.body: He first lays out two facts: the AI companionship track can reach tens of millions of DAU both domestically and overseas, and these companies have all received money, with some already breaking even or slightly profitable. From this he concludes—this is real user demand with commercial value. So why hasn't it exploded? He attributes it to three difficulties: first, the user threshold is too high, requiring great imagination and expression ability, and the younger the age the greater the imagination, so users are confined to younger and ACG circles; second, monetization is difficult, charging Token fees, and Tokens are hard to sell at a high premium, with poor gross margins; third, AI characters are dead and unchanging—chat for ten days and you find this person doesn't change, so long-term retention on a single character is impossible. His solution is to make it into a game: UGC to PGC lowers the threshold, games come with their own business model, and after characters are PGC-ized they can keep growing.

points.h: New platforms only come from new media and new interactions
points.body: He gives a rule he believes no one has broken in twenty years: opportunities for new content platforms only come from new media and new interactions. The differences between information media are very subtle—long video and short video are simply not the same thing, and Xiaohongshu's image-text and Weibo's image-text are not the same thing either; each medium has the content it is best suited to carry and the corresponding interaction form, and only when paired do they correspond to a native platform. He uses this framework to reject Sora: Sora is still short video, the interaction is still up-down swipe, and left-right swipe to see derivative videos is essentially no different from tapping a special effect in Douyin to see videos others made with that effect, so "is this the new Douyin" is absolutely impossible. Conversely, ChatGPT is new media plus new interaction, so it must be a platform.

points.h: Chatbots may strip away your decision rights
points.body: He believes that the future commercial space of Chatbots like ChatGPT may be a business model never seen in human history, and not the advertising push everyone imagines. His conjecture is long-cycle decision control: the ultimate form of twenty years of internet information matching is short video plus Douyin-style interaction, which strips away your information autonomy—you completely cannot decide what you want to watch; Chatbot has the opportunity to strip away another right—the right to make decisions autonomously. You will forget how to make decisions, asking the large model about everything, and this habit will grow deeper and deeper. Ultimately it may not be timely ad pushes, but predicting your future important business decisions, using a relatively long cycle to manipulate your decisions, such as what house to buy, what car to buy, what school to send your child to—when you finally make the decision, it has long predicted it.

He divides Agents into two value orientations. The first is end-to-end replacement, saving your time; this is the core story Manus tells, and all the stories told across Silicon Valley are this—can it replace human labor, move toward full automation, and make large numbers of people unemployed. The second is letting you do things you originally couldn't do, with humans and Agents collaborating: you give it feedback, and it immediately gives you feedback. He explicitly says what he wants to do is the second, and he will care about latency, because there is still another round of processing. He takes web coding as an example: people who completely cannot code really can code things out with a coding agent—this is doing things you couldn't do, and the value is self-evident.

points.h: The gap between domestic and overseas models is widening
points.body: He gives a judgment opposite to the mainstream feeling: over the past year everyone felt the gap between domestic and overseas models was getting smaller, but his feeling is the opposite. The reason is not that the absolute gap is widening, but that those few models were the first to cross some very critical usability points—in 2023 and 2024 domestic models scored 60 and overseas 75, a 15-point gap; today domestic has caught up to 80 and overseas is 90, only a 10-point gap, smaller than before, but between 85 and 88 may be a particularly critical tipping point, and if you haven't crossed it, no matter how close the benchmark scores are, it's meaningless. He adds: today no company doing agents can avoid depending on Claude's models. At the same time different models still have different strengths: for 2C-type tasks use Claude, for front-end drawing switch to Gemini, and in some places you still have to use GPT.

terms.def: Zhang Yueguang believes that merely "couldn't be made without this generation of technology" is not enough; it also requires open input and output.
A product that you can't go back from once used, where the new solution has an all-around advantage over the old one.
Technology that makes 2D illustrations move, common in the game industry.
The work of designing how user input is transformed into model-usable context.
Two product logics: consuming user attention versus saving user time.

quotes.text: I think Miaoya is not an AI native product. It is an internet product that brings AI capabilities into full play.
The product manager's original job, the entire original industry's collaboration and cooperation process, is a very linear thing.

The opportunity for a new content platform comes from only one thing. Only one thing will produce a new content platform—new supply, new human rights, no—it must be new media and new interaction that produce a new platform.
